_help: The Quick guide page. Each rule has an id (used by items in their "topic" field), a title, the rule in one line and one example. "track" (A, B, C or D) decides which study links are shown with it.

sections.title: In-text basics (use these all the time)

rules.title: Parenthetical citation
rules.rule: Author and year both go in brackets, straight after the idea, usually at the end of the sentence. The full stop goes after the bracket.
rules.example: Short study sessions help students remember more (Duarte, 2020).

rules.title: Narrative citation
rules.rule: The author's name is part of the sentence. Only the year goes in brackets. No comma before the bracket.
rules.example: Duarte (2020) found that short study sessions help students remember more.

rules.title: One author
rules.rule: Surname only (no initials), a comma, then the year.
rules.example: (Okafor, 2021)

rules.title: Two authors
rules.rule: Use & inside brackets. Use “and” in the sentence.
rules.example: (Kaur & Novak, 2020) · Kaur and Novak (2020)

rules.title: Three or more authors
rules.rule: First author + et al. from the first citation. Full stop after “al” only. No comma before et al.
rules.example: (Abebe et al., 2022) · Abebe et al. (2022)

rules.title: Group author with an abbreviation
rules.rule: Use the organisation's name when there is no person as author (common for reports and websites). First time: full name + abbreviation in square brackets. After that: the abbreviation only.
rules.example: First: (National Centre for Urban Transport [NCUT], 2021) · Then: (NCUT, 2021)

rules.title: Direct quotation
rules.rule: A direct quotation needs a page: p. for one page, pp. for a range, para. if there are no page numbers (web pages).
rules.example: (Halvorsen, 2016, p. 88) · (Iyer & Brennan, 2019, pp. 12-13) · (Zhou, 2023, para. 6) · Halvorsen (2016, p. 88) stated that “…”

rules.title: Several works in one bracket
rules.rule: Alphabetical order by the first author's surname, separated by semicolons.
rules.example: (Delgado, 2018; Mwangi, 2021)

rules.title: No date
rules.rule: Write n.d. (two full stops) in place of the year.
rules.example: (Varga, n.d.)

rules.title: Page numbers for a paraphrase
rules.rule: APA: a page number for a paraphrase is optional (but helpful). Your course's setting is shown below.
rules.example: (Larsen, 2017) · (Larsen, 2017, p. 31)

sections.title: Less common cases (look these up when you need them)

rules.title: Quotation of 40 words or more
rules.rule: Try not to use long quotations. If you must: start on a new line, indent the whole quotation, no quotation marks. The citation goes after the final full stop, with no full stop after it.
rules.example: … than those who do not. (Moreau, 2019, p. 112)

rules.title: Same author, same year
rules.rule: Add a, b, c after the year. The letters follow the order in your reference list.
rules.example: (Sato, 2020a) · (Sato, 2020b)

rules.title: No author
rules.rule: First check if an organisation is the author. If there is really no author, use the title (shortened if long) in place of the author. Check your course guide for the exact punctuation.
rules.example: (“Rooftop Gardens and City Heat,” 2022)

rules.title: How to write it
rules.rule: The original author first, then “as cited in” and the source you actually read. If the original year is unknown, leave it out.
rules.example: (Varga, 2014, as cited in Osei, 2021) · Varga (2014, as cited in Osei, 2021) found … · (Mwangi, as cited in Halvorsen, 2022)

rules.title: Reference list
rules.rule: Only the source you actually read goes in the reference list.
rules.example: You wrote (Varga, 2014, as cited in Osei, 2021): only Osei (2021) goes in the reference list.

rules.title: When to use it
rules.rule: Only when you cannot get the original (e.g. it is out of print or in a language you cannot read). Reading the original is better.
rules.example: The library has Varga's article online → read it and cite Varga (2014) directly.

rules.title: Strength and stance
rules.rule: Tentative: suggest, propose. Neutral: state, report, note, describe. Strong: argue, claim, assert, maintain. Findings: find, show, demonstrate.
rules.example: Petrova (2021) suggested … · Haddad (2019) argued … · Duarte (2022) found …

rules.title: Represent the author fairly
rules.rule: Choose a verb that matches what the author did: found evidence, gave an opinion, described, or made a careful proposal. Avoid “says” for everything.
rules.example: An experiment → showed. A careful idea → suggested. A strong opinion → argued.

rules.title: Grammar after the verb
rules.rule: Some verbs take a that-clause (argue that, find that). Some take a noun phrase (describe the process, discuss the effects). Do not write “discuss about” or “suggest to”.
rules.example: Okafor (2020) described the process of applying for a visa.

rules.title: According to
rules.rule: “According to Author (year), …” already reports the idea. Do not add a reporting verb.
rules.example: According to Haddad (2019), cities need more green space.

rules.title: Agreement
rules.rule: One author: singular verb (argues, has argued). Two authors or et al.: plural verb (argue, have argued).
rules.example: Moreau (2019) argues … · Abebe et al. (2022) show …

rules.title: Tense
rules.rule: APA prefers the past or present perfect for reporting (argued, has argued). Some courses teach the present simple. Follow your course's setting below.
rules.example: Moreau (2019) argued … · Moreau (2019) argues …

rules.title: Author-first or idea-first?
rules.rule: Author-first (narrative) puts the focus on who said it and lets you choose a reporting verb. Idea-first (parenthetical) puts the focus on the idea.
rules.example: Mensah (2022) found that … · … more on phones (Mensah, 2022).

rules.title: Patterns to mix
rules.rule: Do not end every sentence with (Author, year). Mix several patterns.
rules.example: Lee (2020) argues that … · According to Lee (2020), … · As Lee (2020) notes, … · A study by Lee (2020) found … · … (Lee, 2020).

rules.title: Combining sources that agree
rules.rule: Cite both in one bracket (alphabetical order, semicolon), or name both in the sentence.
rules.example: (Mwangi, 2019; Tran, 2021) · Both Mwangi (2019) and Tran (2021) found …
